title: The Weary Parent
reflection: In which of the five dimensions is parenting costing me more than it used to, and what is one small recharge I could give a place in my day?

questions.q: According to Lesson 8, what does weariness in a parent tell us?
o: That the parent has not tried hard enough in at least one of the five dimensions.
That the parent’s love for the child has begun to weaken, and needs rekindling.
That the supply has run short, and the parent has not in fact failed.
That the parent was made differently from the parents who seem to manage.
questions.e: A store that has run low is not a fault. It is a sign that the supply has run short, and part of that supply lies in the hands of other people and in circumstances. A depleted parent is not a parent who has failed. Weariness announces itself first by effort, when it takes extra effort to discharge the duties of parenthood.
questions.c: Weariness shows that the supply has run short; it is not a failure

questions.q: A parent has felt flat and numb towards her daughter for several weeks, and a sense of hopelessness has crept in. Which response fits Lesson 8?
o: Try harder at all five dimensions, so that the feeling is simply worked through.
Wait for a rest or a holiday, since rest recharges the body and the heart again.
Treat the feeling as guilt, and use it as a spur to do better.
Speak to a doctor, knowing that it is not a verdict on her as a mother.
questions.e: The numbness is not a verdict on the parent. It tells us that the recharging has not been enough for what has been going out. If the flatness or the numbness lasts for weeks, or comes with a sense of hopelessness, please speak to your doctor. Trying harder only spends more of a store that is already low.
questions.c: Flatness that lasts for weeks deserves a doctor, and is no verdict on the parent

questions.q: The parent of two small children cannot take a break. Which kind of recharge does Lesson 8 suggest?
o: A small one: three slow breaths, a warm drink sitting down, or a request for help.
A plan for a week away, to be taken as soon as the children are old enough to be left.
Giving each child a little less for a while, so that more is kept in store for later.
A longer practice each evening, since a small recharge will not be enough to refill the store.
questions.e: Let the recharge be small: three slow breaths, a minute of japa, a warm drink taken sitting down. And ask for help. Other people are one of the sources, and asking is drawing on the source, not a weakness. The warm drink, sitting down, is part of the job, not an extra.
questions.c: A small recharge given a fixed place in the day; asking for help

questions.q: According to Lesson 8, why must the care of the child walk beside the care of the parent?
o: A parent who rests is excused from some of her duties for a time, and the child understands.
A parent who looks after herself is a better example for the child to follow and learn from.
A channel passes on only what it has received; we cannot give what we lack.
A child’s needs grow smaller once the parent’s own needs have been met.
questions.e: Each of us is a channel through which energy flows, and a channel can pass on only what it has received. Let the care of the child walk side by side with the care of yourself, because what we do not have, we cannot give. A rechargeable battery, joined now and then to its power source, renews itself and goes on giving.
questions.c: A parent is a channel: what we do not have, we cannot give

questions.q: “Guilt that says ‘I am not good enough’ is the healthy kind, because it presses a parent harder to improve.”
questions.e: Guilt says, “I did something that was not up to the mark.” Self-blame says, “I am not good enough.” The first speaks of an act, which belongs to the changing personality. The second wrongly says that the person herself is diminished. Guilt is healthy as a spur, but it must never harden into self-blame.
questions.c: Guilt is a spur, never a stick: an act, not me

questions.q: After shouting at her children, a father sits on the stairs thinking, “What kind of father does that?” Which thought fits Lesson 8?
o: “I was not up to the mark, and I must be harder on myself so it does not happen again.”
“That was an act, not me. I have not learned this yet,” and goes back.
“Some fathers are simply not patient, and I am probably one of them.”
“It was the children’s doing, and any parent would have shouted in my place.”
questions.e: A student who slips says, “not yet.” A parent can say it to herself: “That was an act, not me. I have not learned this yet.” Then stand up and go back. You come back to yourself first, with patience, and patience is formed by repetition, impression by impression.
questions.c: A parent is a student: “not yet,” and patience is formed by repetition

questions.q: What does the picture of the clutch of a car teach a parent?
o: To hold back from engaging at all, so that exhaustion is avoided in the first place.
To let the wheels turn freely each time, and never to hold anything back from the child.
To keep engaged without a break, since a parent’s duty never really ends in this life.
To engage fully in duty and, when it is time, to let go of it.
questions.e: Holding the sense of duty together with the larger picture lets us engage fully in our duties and, when it is time, disengage. It is the clutch of the car, which joins the wheels to the engine and releases them again. Let out too fast it jumps; held down it never lets the wheels turn.
questions.c: The clutch: engage fully and, when it is time, let go

questions.q: A parent has done all she can for her son’s schooling, and his results are poor. Which view fits Lesson 8?
o: The results are hers, since she is the main cause of how well her son does at school.
She should do still more, until the results show that all her effort has worked.
The doing is hers, in full; results have many causes, so she holds them lightly.
She should care less about school itself, so that the results can never hurt her.
questions.e: We have a right to action alone, and not to its fruits. An outcome is born of many causes working together. Parents are one cog in a very large machine, and should not take too much credit when things go well, nor blame themselves when they do not. That does not mean growing indifferent or cold toward duty.
questions.c: Hold the results lightly: the doing is ours, the outcome has many causes

questions.q: “When weariness settles in, the first remedy is to try harder to give in all five dimensions.”
questions.e: Trying harder only spends more of a store that is already low. First we notice, by asking in which of the five it is costing more than it used to. Then the care of the child walks beside the care of the parent, and a store that is refilled can go on giving.
questions.c: Notice first; trying harder spends a store already low

questions.q: A parent often looks at other parents and decides that she is behind. Which use of that habit fits Lesson 8?
o: Stop looking at other parents altogether, since the comparison only does harm.
Copy whatever the calmest parent does, until her own ways have been replaced.
Ask other parents where she stands, so that she knows what to improve.
Learn one small thing from what she sees, and not measure herself by it.
questions.e: Our measuring stick grows from reflecting honestly on how we are doing, from watching other parents and learning from them, and from the guidance of our own parents. The habit is already there, and only its use changes: to learn from what you see, not to measure yourself by it. Margaret tried one small thing a calmer neighbour did.
questions.c: Learn from other parents, do not measure yourself by them
